query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges not from conventional bulk intermetallic precipitation or grain coarsening but from stress‐ and temperature‐induced short-range ordering and nanoscale solute segregation along grain boundaries. This subtle, localized chemical partitioning weakens intergranular cohesion, leading to premature crack initiation under service loads.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with homogeneous elemental distribution and no large-scale precipitates.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to controlled thermal aging at elevated temperatures (e.g., 650–750°C) combined with a sustained mechanical load (e.g., creep or fatigue conditions) for varying durations.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation; service-relevant temperatures in the high-temperature regime; mechanical loading conditions representative of engineering service (e.g., cyclic or sustained stress levels); and a time series to capture the evolution of segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale solute segregation and the formation of short-range ordered regions along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature and applied stress enhance element mobility. Under these conditions, even in the absence of classical grain-boundary precipitation, specific solute species in the high-entropy matrix segregate subtly to grain boundaries, creating zones of chemical inhomogeneity. These zones, characterized by short-range order, reduce the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries, thereby promoting brittle fracture despite the alloy retaining its overall single-phase character.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-processed baseline, thermally aged and stressed specimens will exhibit: (1) detectable nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries (via high-resolution atom probe tomography or TEM), (2) a measurable decrease in fracture toughness (via bend or impact testing) without overt formation of large-scale intermetallic phases or significant grain coarsening.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated single-phase alloy showing uniform elemental distribution, high toughness, and absence of conventional brittle precipitates or significant grain coarsening.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be dominant under service conditions that combine high temperature (approaching 650–750°C) and sustained mechanical loading over extended durations. It may not be significant under lower temperatures, very high strain-rate conditions, or in environments where other degradation mechanisms (e.g., oxidation) prevail.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the quantitative relationship between the degree of segregation/short-range order and the reduction in toughness. Furthermore, distinguishing the subtle effects of nanoscale ordering from other possible minor precipitate formation remains challenging without advanced characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one maintained at the as-cast, homogeneous state, and another subjected to controlled thermal aging (650–750°C) with an applied load for varied durations. Utilize high-resolution characterization techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography, high-resolution TEM) to measure grain-boundary composition and detect any signs of short-range order. Simultaneously, perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., bend tests) to quantify changes in mechanical response.
measurements: Fracture toughness or impact energy measurements
Microstructural analyses to confirm absence/presence of large-scale precipitates or grain coarsening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally and mechanically stressed samples do not show any evidence of nanoscale solute segregation or short-range ordering at the grain boundaries, or if there is no corresponding reduction in toughness compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified. Similarly, if conventional precipitation or grain coarsening emerges as the dominant mechanism for toughness degradation, the hypothesis is refuted.
